title: Irish Teen's Eco Purge Invention Tackles Microplastic Pollution
summary: Microplastics are everywhere — in oceans, soil, food, and even the air we breathe. Because they're so tiny, removing them is incredibly difficult. But 18-year-old Arya Satheesh from Ireland has come up with a clever solution. She developed Eco Purge, a plant-based plastic that naturally decomposes while helping break down microplastics already in the environment. Arya first became interested in microplastics in 2024, when she created a water-quality sensor for a national science competition. Her device could detect microplastics in water, but it couldn't remove them. Determined to fix the problem, she began developing Eco Purge. To make the bioplastic, she needed two natural enzymes. Arya contacted several biotechnology companies for samples. Some offered to sell them, but they were too expensive for a high school student. Undeterred, Arya reached out to Professor Kevin O'Connor, a researcher at BiOrbic in Ireland. He obtained the enzyme samples and helped her gain access to a laboratory at a local university, where she could develop Eco Purge. By early 2026, Arya had her first prototype. She tested it by placing a set amount of microplastic with Eco Purge in soil, salt water, and fresh water. She observed the samples for six weeks. To her delight, at the end of the trial, both the microplastic and Eco Purge had decomposed in each sample. Her invention earned her the European regional title at The Earth Prize in May 2026, along with $12,500 in prize money and access to experts to help her develop the project further. Arya still faces challenges before Eco Purge can be widely available — the enzymes only work on certain types of plastic, and high temperatures can damage them. Producing large amounts of enzymes could also be expensive. But she's determined to overcome these hurdles. "Science isn't just about understanding the world," she says. "It's about leaving it better than we found it."
why_it_matters: Arya's project is a reminder that the people solving big environmental problems are not only large companies and governments — a student with a good question, a mentor and lab access can make real progress. It also matters for this generation: if microplastics are already in oceans, soil and human bodies, the cleanup technology being invented now will shape the world today's teenagers inherit.

background_read: Microplastics are pieces of plastic smaller than five millimetres, created when bottles, bags, clothing and tyres break apart — researchers have found them in ocean water, farm soil, rain, and even in human blood and lungs.

Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions, and some bacteria have evolved enzymes that can digest certain plastics; a bacterium able to break down PET, the plastic used in drink bottles, was identified in Japan in 2016, which is what made ideas like Eco Purge possible.

Bioplastics (plastics made from plants such as corn starch instead of oil) do break down eventually, but many of them only do so in special industrial conditions, so a plastic that decomposes in ordinary soil or water would be genuinely unusual.

The Earth Prize (an international competition that gives money and expert support to teenage environmental projects) is one of several youth science awards that have pushed student inventions toward real laboratories rather than leaving them as school projects.

BiOrbic (an Irish research centre that studies how to replace oil-based materials with sustainable bio-based ones) is the type of university lab that normally works with companies rather than with a high school student.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — proof that student scientists can contribute
perspectives.description: Arya got a working prototype, a prize and expert support at an age when most people are still choosing school subjects. Her story shows that research institutions and competitions can open real doors to teenagers who ask the right questions.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — a lab result is not yet a solution
perspectives.description: The trial used a set amount of microplastic in three small samples over six weeks, which is nothing like a real ocean, river or field. Eco Purge also only works on certain plastics, the enzymes are damaged by heat, and producing them in bulk could be very expensive — so calling it a fix for pollution is a big jump.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — the pattern of promising inventions that stall
perspectives.description: Many prize-winning student projects never make it past the lab because the step from prototype to factory is the hardest and most expensive part. It is also worth remembering that cleanup technology treats the symptom, while the flood of new plastic entering the environment each year is the underlying cause.

With prize money and access to experts, the next steps would be testing in real water and soil, finding enzymes that survive higher temperatures, and studying whether the material can be made cheaply at scale. Even if Eco Purge itself does not succeed, the enzymes and methods behind it could feed into other plastic-degrading technologies.
